## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- The judges' era was a dark time for Israel, when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." Bethlehem means "House of Bread." Guzik reads the famine as a sign that Israel was disobeying God (Deut 11), and the move to Moab as a step in the wrong direction. — Guzik
- Dating: since Boaz's mother was Rahab, Ellicott places the story early in the judges' period. Wesley agrees and notes that Christ came from two Gentile women. Gill sets out many competing dates. Pulpit says guessing the date is pointless. — Ellicott; Wesley; Gill; Pulpit
- "Sojourn" means living somewhere as a foreigner. NET notes it is unclear whether the move was meant to be temporary. Gill takes it as temporary, until the famine ended. — Pulpit; NET https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Rut+1%3A1-6&theme=false; Gill
- *Was Elimelech wrong to leave? Writers disagree:*
  - **Against him:** Ellicott says leaving God's land for the land of the god Chemosh was "doubtful" and broke the spirit of God's law. Henry calls it a distrustful, discontented spirit that set a bad example. Ligonier says Elimelech tried to "read providence" when he should have stayed and repented; it treats the famine as a covenant warning-curse. Piper calls the move "playing with fire." — Ellicott; Henry; https://ligonier.org/learn/articles/3-things-ruth; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ruth-sweet-and-bitter-providence
  - **More neutral:** NET says the famine does not necessarily mean Bethlehem was under God's discipline, only that it was severe. It also notes that God never forbade seeking food abroad, and once sent his people abroad in a famine (Gen 37–50). — NET https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=1 and the 1:1-6 page above

**v. 2**
- Elimelech means "God is King." Pulpit says it is not "My God is King," though Gill and NET read it "my God is king." NET thinks naming him explicitly casts him in a good light. Guzik says he did not live as if God were his king. — Pulpit; Gill; NET; Guzik
- Naomi means "pleasant." Pulpit argues it means "God is sweet," which sets up v. 20. — Ellicott; Pulpit
- Mahlon and Chilion are linked to words for sickness and wasting. They may have been sickly, which would fit their early deaths. — Ellicott; Wesley; NET
- Ephrathites: Ephrath was an old name for Bethlehem (Gill, Wesley). NET says the word elsewhere refers to a clan living near Bethlehem, as with David's father (1 Sam 17:12). — Gill; Wesley; NET

**v. 3**
- Gill thinks Elimelech died soon after they arrived. Pulpit notes the text attaches no blame to him. Guzik says it is hard to call his death God's direct judgment, but the move clearly didn't help: "you bring yourself with you." — Gill; Pulpit; Guzik

**v. 4**
- *Were the Moabite marriages sinful? Writers disagree:*
  - **Yes:** Guzik says they disobeyed God's command not to marry pagans. Ellicott says the sons carried on their father's fault, and cites the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) saying they broke God's decree. — Guzik; Ellicott
  - **Maybe not:** Gill mentions the view that the wives became converts before marrying, and says God permitted the marriages so that the Messiah would come from one of them. Wesley says either the wives were converts or the sons sinned and were punished. — Gill; Wesley
  - **No blame in the text:** Pulpit says the book never hints at condemnation. In its view the ban in Deut 7:3 concerned Canaanites, a different case from Moabites living in their own land. — Pulpit
- Names: Ellicott takes Ruth as "companion" or "comeliness." Pulpit rejects meanings like "beauty" and "rose." Jewish legend made Ruth a daughter of King Eglon; Ellicott and Gill both reject this. — Ellicott; Pulpit; Gill
- Ligonier notes that Moabites were barred from "the assembly of the Lord" (Deut 23). — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/who-was-ruth

**v. 5**
- *Were the deaths a punishment?* The Targum says the sons' days were cut short for breaking God's decree (Gill). Ellicott says it is "not for us to say." Pulpit sees no sign of God's displeasure and warns against assuming it, citing the tower of Siloam (Luke 13:1-5). — Gill; Ellicott; Pulpit
- A childless widow was among the most helpless people in the ancient world. Wesley says only God can comfort such loss. NET notes an unusual word for "sons" here that links to the book's ending (4:16). — Guzik; Wesley; NET

**v. 6**
- The Hebrew word *paqad* ("visited," "attended to") means God took note of his people and cared for them. "Bread" here means crops, the reversal of the famine. — Pulpit; NET (both pages above)
- Ellicott suggests Naomi's conscience may have troubled her. Henry says that once the reason for being in a bad place ends, staying becomes sin. Guzik praises her for acting on the news rather than just wishing. — Ellicott; Henry; Guzik

**v. 7**
- Both daughters-in-law meant to go all the way, not just see her off. Ellicott compares Orpah to Pliable in *Pilgrim's Progress*. Pulpit says the love between them reflects well on Naomi's household. — Ellicott; Pulpit

**v. 8**
- "Mother's house": mothers and daughters were close and shared women's quarters (Gill, Wesley). NET says it was more fitting for widows to return to their mothers. — Gill; Wesley; NET
- "Loving devotion" (or "deal kindly") translates *hesed*, the Hebrew word for loyal kindness. Henry notes that Naomi names the LORD (Jehovah) in her parting blessing. — Guzik; Henry

**v. 9**
- Naomi gives a double blessing, using the LORD's name twice. Guzik says marriage is meant to be a place of "rest." NET explains the unusual grammar ("may He enable you to find rest"). — Ellicott; Guzik; NET; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_19-13

**v. 10**
- "We will *return* with you": for the moment the young women speak as if Judah were their own home. — Pulpit

**v. 11**
- Naomi is referring to the levirate custom, in which a dead man's brother married the widow (Deut 25:5). Piper says this prepares for how the story turns later. — Guzik; Wesley; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ruth-sweet-and-bitter-providence

**v. 12**
- NET suggests Naomi may be exaggerating for emphasis. — NET

**v. 13**
- Ellicott and NET prefer the translation "it is far more bitter for me than for you." Precept Austin notes the same Hebrew word comes back as "Mara" in v. 20. "The hand of the LORD" means Naomi admits God is in control. — Ellicott; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_19-13
- Wesley takes it as "It is with me that God has a controversy," and says we should hear God's correction as if it were spoken only to us. — Wesley
- Guzik says Naomi was not bitter against God and was returning in repentance (compare v. 20). — Guzik

**v. 14**
- "Clung" suggests strong commitment. — NET
- Orpah:
  - Wesley: she loved Naomi, but not enough to leave her country. Many value Christ in the same way yet fall short.
  - Ellicott: comfort and home held her back.
  - Guzik: both women felt the same, but Ruth *acted*. He also reports a rabbinic legend that Orpah became Goliath's ancestor.
  - NET: Orpah is "commendable and devoted."
  — Wesley; Ellicott; Guzik; NET

**v. 15**
- *What did Naomi believe about "her gods"?*
  - Ellicott: Naomi saw the Moabite idols as real powers limited to Moab, and was not enlightened enough to see the LORD as more than Israel's God. — Ellicott
  - Ligonier disagrees: her prayer in vv. 8-9 shows she believed the LORD acts outside Israel, so the remark was likely meant to persuade. Pulpit likewise says the LORD ruled in Moab too. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ruth-and-naomi; Pulpit
- Wesley: Naomi was testing Ruth, and hinting that following her meant taking up the true religion. — Wesley

**v. 16**
- Ruth chose to leave Moab's gods for Israel's God. Guzik credits Naomi's faithfulness in hard times, not her compromise, and quotes Spurgeon that compromise wins no one. — Guzik
- Gill: "Your God" means Jehovah, not Chemosh. He applies the verse to a soul that clings to Christ. — Gill
- Henry: "Entreat me not" can mean "Be not against me." People who hold us back from God act as our enemies, even if they are family. — Henry
- *Grace or choice? A difference in emphasis:*
  - Ligonier (Reformed) says Ruth's confession could come "only" from God's grace giving her new life (John 3), and quotes Henry on grace inclining the soul to choose. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ruth-and-naomi
  - Guzik and Wesley stress acting on one's love and loving Christ "enough" (see v. 14).
- Piper: Ruth heard Naomi say God was dealing bitterly with her, and still wanted Naomi's God. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/bitter-providence-and-barley-harvest

**v. 17**
- NET weighs two readings: "not even death will part us" against "only death will part us," and favours the second. The oath formula is an idiom of commitment; it does not mean God was bound to punish her. — NET https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Rut+1%3A16-17
- Ellicott: Ruth swears by the name of Israel's God. Wesley: she wanted to be buried with Naomi, in hope that they would rise together. — Ellicott; Wesley

**v. 18**
- Naomi only stopped arguing; she did not fall silent toward Ruth. Wesley says half-resolve invites temptation, while firm resolve shuts the door. — NET; Wesley

**v. 19**
- The journey was at least 50 miles and crossed two rivers. Grief had aged Naomi. "They said" is feminine in Hebrew, so it was the women of the town speaking. — Ellicott; Wesley; Guzik

**v. 20**
- The wordplay: Naomi means pleasant, Mara means bitter. "The Almighty" is *Shaddai*, possibly "All-Sufficient," the One who gives and takes back. — Ellicott; NET; Pulpit (v. 2)
- *How should we judge Naomi's words?*
  - Guzik: honest and repentant, not bitter against God. — Guzik
  - Precept Austin (an older writer it quotes): she forgets her own part and "seems to charge the Almighty." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_119-22
  - Piper: so embittered she can't see God's mercy, yet her words are "not false." He adds that she would not dodge the problem by saying "the devil caused the famine." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ruth-sweet-and-bitter-providence; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/when-suffering-comes
  - Henry: we should let our hearts be humbled by humbling providences. — Henry

**v. 21**
- "Full" means her husband, sons and property. "Testified against me" is a courtroom image of God giving sentence. — Wesley
- NET: "empty" is ironic, since faithful Ruth is standing right beside her. NET notes the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) reads "humbled me," and rejects it. — NET; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_119-22
- Henry: there is a spiritual fullness that cannot be taken away. — Henry

**v. 22**
- They arrive at the barley harvest, about late April. God has restored plenty, and NET says this raises the question of whether he will do the same for these two women. — Ellicott; NET
- Guzik: everything good in the chapters that follow starts from Naomi's return. — Guzik
